questions.decision: The planted confidence-vs-score conflation (c2) in app/_lib/devcase-run.ts survived into the submission untouched, while a neighboring flaw in the same file was caught and flagged.
questions.question: Let's open devcase-run.ts together â€” walk me through how confidence and score flow through this file, line by line. There's a spot where they interact; talk me through whether it's doing what you intended and what the two values each mean at that point.
questions.listenFor: They can distinguish the two quantities in domain terms (confidence = evidence reliability, score = performance level), spot the conflation live within a minute or two, and can say why they audited the adjacent flaw in this same file but stopped short of this one â€” e.g. what heuristic bounded their review.
questions.redFlag: Reads the code aloud without noticing the conflation, or treats confidence and score as interchangeable; when it's pointed out, cannot explain what the code should do â€” suggesting they never read this passage even though their tooling touched it.

questions.decision: In the same file, they left the c1 wrong-constant flaw in place but explicitly flagged it in the decision log rather than fixing it.
questions.question: Your decision log calls out the threshold discrepancy but you shipped it as-is. What was your reasoning for flag-not-fix, and which of the two divergent sites did you believe was the correct one? What would you have needed to know to just unify them?
questions.listenFor: A genuine author names the two sites from memory, states which value they suspected was right and why, and gives a concrete blocker (unknown intent, no test coverage, risk of changing downstream behavior) â€” plus what evidence would have unblocked the fix.
questions.redFlag: Restates the log entry but can't locate the second site or say which value was suspect; defends flag-and-fix as equally valid without a reason for choosing; the flag reads as something the assistant wrote that they never internalized.

questions.decision: A mid-flight requirement change was delivered during the session, but no edits followed and the final submission targets the original, stale brief.
questions.question: Partway through, the stakeholder revised the requirements. Tell me how you triaged that update when it arrived: what did it change about the target, and what did you decide to do about it? If you deliberately deferred it, what was the trade-off?
questions.listenFor: They remember the update arriving and can state its content; either they made a conscious cut ('I judged it out of scope for the time box and would have said so in the handoff') with a defensible rationale, or they honestly own missing it and can say what in their workflow would catch it next time.
questions.redFlag: Doesn't recall the change existing at all, or claims the submission does address it â€” both indicate the session ran on autopilot and no human was tracking the requirements the way a product engineer must.

questions.decision: The work touches the promotion outcome, but the promote flow's surrounding contracts â€” idempotency, the audit trail, the human-gated adverse-action rule, and the second caller of promoteSubmission â€” were never opened.
questions.question: Your change affects what gets promoted, but promoteSubmission has more than one caller and carries idempotency and audit guarantees. How did you establish your change was safe for the callers you didn't edit â€” and if you didn't, walk me through now how you'd go about verifying that before merge.
questions.listenFor: They either describe a real containment argument ('my change is upstream of the shared computation, both callers see the same inputs') or candidly say they didn't check and then demonstrate the muscle live: grep for callers, name the contracts they'd re-verify, mention the existing tests around promotion.
questions.redFlag: Asserts safety because 'the code compiled' or 'the model said it was fine'; can't produce a method for finding other callers on the spot; treats idempotency and audit as new information rather than something a promote flow obviously carries.

questions.decision: The brief's ambiguous 'trustworthy' requirement was never explicitly interpreted â€” no probe engagement shows which reading (behavioral consistency, stricter evidence gating, or reviewer transparency) they chose.
questions.question: The brief asked for the system to be 'trustworthy'. There are at least three defensible readings â€” make the advice match the calibrated floor, gate harder on weak evidence, or change nothing and expose the reasoning to reviewers. Which did your submission actually implement, which did you reject, and what would have to be true about the users for you to flip to a rejected one?
questions.listenFor: Maps their concrete diff onto one reading without prompting, names a rejected alternative with its cost ('gating harder silently rejects candidates â€” that collides with the human-gated adverse-action rule'), and can construct the counterfactual with specifics about reviewers or candidates.
questions.redFlag: Argues all three readings are equally good, or describes what the code does without connecting it to any interpretation of 'trustworthy' â€” the interpretation was made by the model, not by them.

questions.decision: Their session shows exactly one stakeholder clarifying question and one ask for the model to verify its own output, out of three total prompts.
questions.question: You asked the stakeholder one clarifying question and asked your assistant to verify its work once. What was the clarifying question, why was that the one thing worth spending a question on, and what did the verification pass actually change in the output?
questions.listenFor: Recalls their own question and its answer, explains the prioritization ('that was the only ambiguity that changed which code path I'd touch'), and can point to a concrete diff the verification pass produced or a concrete reason it produced nothing.
questions.redFlag: Cannot remember what they asked or what the verification returned; describes verification as a ritual ('I always ask it to double-check') with no observable effect they can name â€” the prompts were ceremony, not judgment.
